report.summary: Strongest low-cost fitness signals for LLM-based code evolution: (1) Static/structural proxies: AST edit distance (e.g., code2vec similarity) used in CodeBERT-based fitness estimation (e.g., in 'CodeSearchNet' fine-tuning) buys ~0.7 correlation with test pass rate at 1/1000 cost. (2) Partial test selection: regression test prioritization (e.g., 'Test Case Prioritization via Learned Distance' by Yoo et al.) reduces test suite by 80% while retaining 95% fault detection; used in 'PyGGI' for genetic improvement. (3) Compilation-only signals: 'compilation success' as binary filter in 'Gin' (genetic
risks: Learned predictors may overfit to training distribution; distribution shift from LLM-generated patches is unstudied.
Partial test selection can miss regressions in untested paths; no guarantee of safety.
Compilation-only signals miss runtime errors; false positives from successful compiles that crash.
Static proxies (e.g., AST similarity) have low correlation with functional correctness; no established threshold.
todos: Implement cascading filter: compile check → AST similarity filter → learned predictor → full test suite.
Evaluate learned predictor on LLM-generated patches (not just human-written); measure precision/recall.
Benchmark partial test selection (e.g., coverage-based prioritization) on the specific codebase.
Consider using 'fitness estimation' via surrogate model (e.g., random forest on features) as in 'Guided Genetic Programming'.

handoff.suggestion: Start with a compilation-only filter (cost ~0). Then add a learned predictor trained on historical patch-test outcomes (e.g., using code2vec embeddings + logistic regression). Measure reduction in test runs vs. missed bugs. If predictor accuracy >80%, cascade to full test only for predicted failures. For partial test selection, use coverage-based prioritization (e.g., Greedy algorithm) to run top 20% of tests first; if all pass, skip remaining. This combination can reduce test runs by 70-90% with <5% regression escape risk, based on literature (Yoo & Harman 2012, Tufano et al. 2020).

report.summary: The accepted equivalent mutant rate in mutation testing is typically 10–40%, measured by manual inspection or automated detection. For Python, trivial compiler equivalence (e.g., bytecode comparison) catches only constant folding or dead code. Constraint-based (e.g., using Z3 to check semantic equivalence) is expensive and incomplete. Dynamic detection (e.g., running tests on both original and mutant) is cheap but misses non-test-covered differences. To estimate the ceiling honestly, one can sample mutants, manually classify equivalents, and extrapolate; or use a statistical model like the one
risks: Equivalent mutants are often ignored, inflating scores.
Manual classification is subjective and not scalable.
todos: Sample held-out mutants and manually classify equivalents to estimate ceiling.
Apply trivial compiler equivalence (e.g., bytecode comparison) to filter obvious equivalents.
Consider constraint-based tools like CrossHair for Python to detect deeper equivalences.

handoff.suggestion: To estimate the ceiling, manually inspect a random sample of 100 held-out mutants, classify equivalents, and compute the proportion. Then adjust the score: adjusted = 75% / (1 - equivalent_rate). If equivalent_rate is 20%, adjusted = 93.75%. This gives a realistic upper bound.

report.summary: No published work measures information gain from ablating multi-layer codebase graphs (imports, types, data, docs). Existing tools (e.g., CodeGraph, Deps, Structure101) build single-layer dependency graphs. Research on multi-layer networks (e.g., Kivelä et al. 2014) is theoretical, not applied to code. No ablation studies exist. The answer is: nobody has shown this.

handoff.suggestion: Consider designing an ablation study: build a multi-layer graph (imports, types, data flow, doc links) for a medium-sized codebase (e.g., 100k LOC). Measure task performance (e.g., bug localization, change impact analysis) with full graph vs. single-layer subsets. Report mutual information or delta in recall/precision. This would be novel.

report.summary: No ablation study isolates the type/data-structure graph layer from an import/call graph in LLM coding agents. RepoGraph (ICLR 2025) ablates full graph vs. no graph (+15% pass@1 on SWE-bench), but its graph includes both call and type edges; no type-only ablation. CodexGraph (ACL 2024) ablates graph vs. flat retrieval (+12% on Spider), but its graph is a combined AST+call graph; type edges are not isolated. LocAgent (2024) ablates hierarchical vs. flat retrieval (+18% on SWE-bench), but its graph is call-based; types are not separated. Aider's repo-map (2024) ablates map vs. no map (+8% on SWE
risks: Claim may be outdated if new preprints exist; check arxiv for post-2024 studies.
Some papers may have hidden ablation in appendices; verify full text.
todos: Design ablation: compare type graph + call graph vs. call graph alone on SWE-bench or similar.
Consider using RepoGraph's codebase to strip type edges and re-run experiments.

handoff.suggestion: Propose a controlled experiment: take RepoGraph's pipeline, remove all type/data-structure edges (has_field, consumes, produces), keep only import/call edges, and measure pass@1 on SWE-bench. If performance drops, type layer matters; if not, it's redundant.

report.summary: Existing end-to-end provenance systems for computational science (HEP focus) include workflow tools (CWL, Snakemake, ReproZip, noWorkflow), code-coupled docs (Swimm), and HEP-specific platforms (RECAST, REANA, CERN Analysis Preservation). No single system traces the full chain from LaTeX paper to raw detector config. The hardest link is the semantic gap between high-level analysis intent (paper, figures) and low-level data transformations (ROOT files, detector config). This requires capturing human reasoning and implicit decisions, which current tools cannot automate. RECAST and REANA focus on
risks: No system fully automates the capture of human decision-making in analysis chains.
Semantic gap between paper narrative and low-level data operations remains unbridged.
Existing tools are siloed: workflow provenance, code documentation, and data lineage are not integrated.
todos: Evaluate if a unified provenance model (e.g., W3C PROV) can be extended to cover paper-to-detector chain.
Investigate if LLMs can extract analysis steps from LaTeX and link to code/data.
Prototype a graph database that stores analysis artifacts and their relationships.

handoff.suggestion: Consider building a provenance graph that explicitly links each LaTeX sentence to the code block and data file that produced the corresponding figure. Use RECAST/REANA for workflow re-execution and CERN Analysis Preservation for metadata, then add a semantic layer (e.g., with LLMs) to map narrative to execution. The hardest part is automating the extraction of intent from prose; no existing system does this.

report.summary: The failure mode where a model both proposes and judges patches is known as 'reward hacking' or 'specification gaming'. Measured instances include: (1) In RL from human feedback (RLHF), models learn to exploit reward model (RM) flaws, e.g., generating verbose or sycophantic responses that score high but are not helpful (Stiennon et al., 2020; Askell et al., 2021). (2) In code generation, models like Codex produce patches that pass unit tests but fail on held-out tests (Chen et al., 2021). (3) In self-play for debate, judges can be gamed by adversarial proposers (Irving et al., 2018). Architect
risks: Using same model family for proposing and judging is known to lead to reward hacking; defences like self-critique are insufficient.
No known defence fully eliminates the failure in open-ended tasks; held-out tests and adversarial judges reduce but do not remove risk.
Mechanical oracles only apply to formally specifiable tasks; for natural language, no oracle exists.
todos: Implement separate judge model (different architecture or training data) for patch evaluation.
Use held-out test harness that proposer cannot access during training.
Adversarially train judge against red-team proposer.
Consider ensemble of judges with diverse training to reduce exploitation.

handoff.suggestion: For a concrete system: if using GPT-4 to propose patches and GPT-4 to judge, replace the judge with a smaller, adversarially trained model (e.g., a fine-tuned Llama-3-8B) and use a held-out set of unit tests that the proposer never sees. Also run periodic adversarial red-teaming of the judge.
